My Story

I grew up in Vadodara, Gujarat, where my father prioritised an English medium education despite financial challenges. That decision helped open the same path for my three siblings and seven cousins.

I married at nineteen with a diploma in Computer Science and Engineering and later became a mother to two boys. My interest in continuing my education stayed with me. With my husband’s wholehearted support, I joined the University of North Texas to pursue my bachelor’s degree, working toward becoming the first woman in my family’s generation to earn one.

Today, I’m developing my work in product design, analytics and storytelling. My experience in business, motherhood and life across cultures shapes how I understand people’s needs and approach practical problems.

Product Strategy & Experience Design

VHW.ai

A hiring platform concept addressing verification, transparency and workforce oversight.

Verified Human Workforce is a proposed hiring platform connecting candidate verification, job requisitions and workforce reporting. I independently developed the concept, product presentation, visual assets and interactive prototype, and personally delivered the pitch that secured QSTP incubation approval.

RoleProduct creator and designer
ScopeConcept, workflows, prototype and pitch
OutcomeQSTP incubation approval

Hiring Transparency and Verification Gaps

The pitch identified a shared problem with different consequences for each participant.

  • Candidates: time spent applying to ghost jobs or roles whose hiring status is unclear, often without feedback.
  • Employers: irrelevant or duplicate applications, manual reporting and a loss of candidate confidence.
  • Government: unreliable workforce information that makes oversight and nationalization reporting more difficult.

Workflow Architecture and Product Requirements

Link Postings to a Requisition

The proposal connects each posting to a real requisition ID, making the hiring requirement traceable rather than treating a published advert as sufficient evidence of an open position.

Label the Purpose of a Posting

Open, Internal Transfer and Compliance Only categories would tell candidates what kind of opportunity they are considering before they invest time in an application.

Create a Verified Career Profile

A proposed Career Passport would support identity verification and reduce duplicate profiles. National identity connections remain a proposed integration requiring authorization and implementation.

Design Separate Stakeholder Workflows

Candidate application journeys, employer requisition management and government oversight require different views of the same hiring activity. The prototype provides a way to examine those distinct experiences.

Business Model and Adoption Strategy

The pitch combines a government supported infrastructure model with employer subscriptions for compliance dashboards, analytics and reporting. Core candidate access would be free.

The proposed rollout starts with Qatar enterprise pilots before broader adoption and regional expansion. Funding, pilot partnerships and national deployment were requests or roadmap items in the pitch, rather than secured outcomes.

Interactive Product Demonstration

Use “Access Portals” inside the prototype to navigate the stakeholder journeys. This is a demonstration of the proposed experience, not evidence of live identity verification or government integration.

If your browser blocks the embedded preview, open the prototype in a separate tab ↗.

Product Ownership and Incubation Outcome

I prepared the product concept, Figma prototype, Photoshop and Canva visual assets, business presentation and video pitch. I personally pitched VHW.ai to Qatar Science & Technology Park and secured incubation approval.

I also developed related academic projects in Python fraud detection, NLP resume matching and MySQL recruitment reporting.

Validation Priorities and Implementation Roadmap

A pilot would need to test whether posting labels improve candidate understanding, whether verification reduces duplicate profiles, and whether employers can maintain accurate requisition information without excessive administration.

Further work should evaluate matching fairness, feedback quality, privacy requirements and the permissions needed for national identity and regulatory integrations.

Independent Analytical Project

Understanding U.S. Airline Flight Delays

Using visual analysis to compare airline performance and investigate delay patterns.

I used Power BI to prepare flight data, investigate delay patterns and develop visualizations connecting airline performance, flight distance and airport location.

DataFlights, airlines and airports
ToolPower BI
OutputExploratory analysis and interactive visuals

Operational Performance and Delay Drivers

  • How do average arrival delays differ across airlines?
  • Which recorded delay cause contributes the most minutes?
  • Do longer flights show higher delay spikes?

The project also examined airport locations to identify geographic patterns in the analyzed data.

Data Integration and Preparation

I combined a flight dataset containing delays, distances and delay causes with airline names and airport coordinates.

Preparation included removing cancelled and diverted flights, dropping records with missing delay fields, retaining the recorded delay categories and standardizing column names. Airline names and coordinates made the resulting charts and map easier to interpret.

Removing incomplete and disrupted flights defines the scope of this analysis. The results do not describe the full passenger disruption experience.

Dashboard Design and Analytical Methodology

A distance histogram established the concentration of flights between roughly 300 and 1,000 miles. Early airline comparisons and delay cause charts helped guide the final views.

Airline Comparison

A common baseline makes differences in average arrival delay visible across carriers.

Distance and Arrival Delay

A scatter plot exposes concentration and unusual delay values without reducing the relationship to a single average.

Airport Geography

A bubble map places airport delay measures in geographic context.

The Power BI report included hover tooltips, airline and airport filters, and cross highlighting. The images below are static views of those visuals.

Performance Findings

Frontier and American Eagle show higher average arrival delays in the analyzed sample, while Delta and Alaska show lower values. These comparisons are descriptive and do not adjust for route mix or operating conditions.

Most observations cluster at shorter distances. Some longer flights show large delay spikes, but this chart alone does not establish that longer distance causes delays or increases average delay.

The map highlights geographic differences in average delays, including several higher delay locations in the eastern United States. Weather and airport congestion data would be needed to investigate explanations.

The presentation also identifies late aircraft as the largest recorded delay category in the analyzed data.

Scope, Limitations and Further Analysis

The dataset does not cover a full year and lacks weather severity and airport traffic measures. Results therefore describe the analyzed sample rather than current airline performance or seasonal patterns.

Future work would add weather and congestion data, examine time of day and seasonality, and assess whether the data supports a delay prediction model. Statistical significance and causal explanations are not established by these visual comparisons.

Power BI analysis and visualizations by Gazala Shaikh.

Brand Strategy & Campaign Design / Independent Concept

Make Room for You

Campaign strategy connecting household responsibilities with personal ambition.

I developed an exploratory campaign concept examining the thinking behind household routines and the interests women want to pursue alongside family life. Existing Apple products appear as tools for creative and personal activities.

My WorkResearch and campaign concept
DeliverablesCase study and visual presentation
StatusConcept developed; evaluation pending

Audience Needs and Campaign Opportunity

Household management involves anticipating needs, remembering commitments and making decisions, as well as completing visible tasks. The research asked how a visual campaign could acknowledge that effort while respectfully representing personal interests and ambitions.

A second question guided the product role: where could technology make a useful contribution without overstating its ability to provide time, childcare, employment or family support?

Research Inputs and Qualitative Perspectives

I reviewed research on cognitive household labor and care responsibilities, alongside written responses from two participants to five open questions. The questions explored routines, challenges, developed abilities, less visible responsibilities and personal ambitions.

This was an exploratory convenience sample. The accounts informed the creative direction but do not establish representative findings about women or homemakers. Product usage was not established.

Campaign Positioning and Creative Direction

The research suggested several expressions of personal fulfillment, including creative exploration and future work. I developed three connected campaign directions rather than defining success only through paid employment or leisure.

Room to Explore

Photography and outdoor discovery, with the device supporting the activity rather than defining the person.

Room to Create

A return to an artistic interest, giving attention to the idea and the act of making.

Room to Begin

Preparation for a personal project or future work opportunity, without suggesting a guaranteed employment outcome.

Campaign Assets

Realistic environments, concise copy and a consistent typographic hierarchy connect the three directions.

Concept imagery generated for this independent portfolio presentation. Scenes are illustrative and are not photographs of the research participants or evidence of their product usage.

Evaluation Framework and Validation Plan

The presentation establishes the proposed campaign direction. Audience response, visual clarity and the relevance of the product scenarios have not yet been evaluated.

The planned next step is participant review of the interpretation, followed by viewer feedback on clarity, credibility and tone. I would use that feedback to revise the compositions. No improvements in wellbeing or employment are claimed.

Research References

Daminger (2019), The cognitive dimension of household labor. Read paper.

Aviv and colleagues (2025; first published online 2024), Cognitive household labor. Read paper.

International Labour Organization (2024), Unpaid care work and labor market participation. Read source.

Tableau / Project

Technology Stock Price Visualization

A time series comparison of Apple, Amazon and Alphabet closing prices.

Analytical Task

Compare recorded closing prices for AAPL, AMZN and GOOGL between 2013 and 2018 using a shared time axis.

Visualization Decisions

I created a Tableau line chart, assigning a distinct color to each company and using an interactive legend to show or hide series. Light gridlines and labeled axes support comparison without overwhelming the data.

Interpretation and Scope

The chart compares nominal share prices. Differences in share price alone do not establish investment performance or company value. A return comparison would require a consistent baseline and treatment of stock splits and dividends.

Case StudyBack to Archive ×

Excel and Tableau / Project

Global Box Office Visualization

Data preparation and visual comparison of film lifetime revenues.

Data Preparation

I prepared Box Office Mojo data in Excel, removing currency symbols and commas, converting revenue fields to numeric values and standardizing column headers before importing it into Tableau.

Visual Analysis

The report uses a horizontal bar chart to rank leading films, a line chart to group revenue by year and a pie chart to compare five selected titles. Each chart addresses a different comparison: ranking, temporal distribution or composition.

Interpretation and Scope

The five film percentages describe the selected titles rather than their share of all global box office revenue. Lifetime gross grouped by release year also differs from revenue earned during each calendar year. These distinctions limit industry growth conclusions. Revenue should not be described as profit without cost data.

MySQL / Independent Project

VHW.ai Relational Database

A ten entity data model for a traceable hiring workflow.

Business Requirements

The project models candidate registration, employer postings, applications, interviews, verification checks and hiring decisions. Payroll, benefits and post employment performance management are outside its scope.

Schema Design

Ten entities connect the workflow: Candidate, CandidateIdentity, Employer, Job, Application, Interview, Verification, HiringDecision, User and AuditLog. Application resolves the many to many relationship between candidates and jobs.

Integrity Rules

The documented SQL uses primary and foreign keys, a unique candidate and job pair to prevent duplicate applications, a unique candidate reference in CandidateIdentity and a unique application reference in HiringDecision.

Reporting

Ten reporting queries use joins, grouping, filtering and aggregation to examine application demand, verification status, interview feedback, hiring outcomes and audit activity. A left join identifies applications without a hiring decision.

Implementation Scope

The submission includes CREATE TABLE statements, sample inserts and result screenshots. This is an academic database implementation, separate from the broader product prototype and proposed integrations. A user role field and an audit table alone do not establish enforced access permissions or automatic audit logging.

Example Reporting Query

Summarize verification records by type and status.

SELECT VerificationType, Status, COUNT(*) AS TotalCount
FROM Verification
GROUP BY VerificationType, Status
ORDER BY VerificationType, Status;

Information Research & Source Evaluation

Documents in Motion

Evaluating research for families navigating international relocation.

Audience and Purpose

I evaluated three academic articles for internationally relocating families, focusing on the usefulness of each source for a specific audience rather than topic similarity alone.

Evaluation Approach

The bibliography examines online information credibility, public libraries as potential community resources, and family archives as a way to preserve documents and cultural memory. Each evaluation considers relevance, accessibility and limitations.

Research Synthesis

Community experience can add context, while official sources establish requirements. Libraries may help newcomers locate information and support, though services vary. Family records have practical and cultural value during relocation.

Communication Opportunities

The synthesis proposes a checklist for evaluating online advice, a directory of community resources and a guide to organizing family records. These are proposed applications of the research, not completed or tested services.

Case StudyBack to VHW.ai ×

Python / Machine Learning / VHW.ai Component

Fake Job Posting Detection

A classification pipeline combining job posting text with structural features.

Related: VHW.ai product case study

Problem and Scope

Identify potentially fraudulent job postings using a labeled dataset. This classifier is a technical component of the VHW.ai initiative, distinct from the broader product prototype and proposed government integrations.

Data and Features

The report documents text normalization, HTML and special character removal, and stopword processing. Engineered features include description and requirement lengths, urgency terms and remote role indicators. These complement TF-IDF representations of posting text.

Model Design

The final model uses Logistic Regression in a unified text and numeric pipeline. A stratified train and test split preserves class proportions, and the pipeline is fitted on training data before test evaluation.

Evaluation Tradeoff

The displayed default confusion matrix contains 3,400 true negatives, 3 false positives, 129 false negatives and 44 true positives. This corresponds to about 25.4% recall for fraudulent postings at that operating point. The displayed ROC AUC is 0.93, a measure of ranking performance rather than the percentage of fraud detected.

Threshold Tuning

The project compares probability thresholds to increase fraud recall. A lower threshold can flag more fraudulent postings, with potential costs in false positives and review workload. The presentation includes adjusted confusion matrices, but production suitability would require validation beyond the submitted test data.

Interpretation and Next Steps

Text and structural patterns support investigation; they do not prove that a posting is fraudulent. Additional work should examine leakage, changing language, subgroup performance and the operational review process before deployment.

Source: VHW.ai technical report and model evaluation presentation. Research implementation; not deployed within the live prototype.

Case StudyBack to VHW.ai ×

Python / NLP / VHW.ai Component

Resume Matching & Candidate Feedback

TF-IDF similarity scoring with visible keyword overlap.

Related: VHW.ai product case study

Problem and Scope

Provide a candidate with an understandable comparison between a resume and job descriptions. The project focuses on explaining textual alignment rather than making an automated hiring decision.

Method

Resumes and job descriptions are represented using TF-IDF vectors. Cosine similarity ranks job descriptions against a selected resume. Shared keywords provide an explanation of why a match appears in the results.

Feedback Design

The presentation converts similarity percentages into five descriptive bands: below 10%, 10–19%, 20–29%, 30–39% and 40% or more. These are project defined interpretation bands, not validated probabilities of suitability or hiring success.

Output

The submitted examples show ranked match scores and overlapping terms. Making those terms visible helps a user inspect the basis of a recommendation and recognize where language differs.

Limits and Further Evaluation

Lexical overlap can miss synonyms and context, reward repeated keywords and understate transferable skills. The materials do not establish ranking quality against expert judgments, fairness across groups or improvements in employment outcomes. Further evaluation should test relevance, explanation quality and the interpretation of score labels.

Source: VHW.ai technical report and model evaluation presentation. Research implementation; not deployed within the live prototype.

Writing & ResearchBack to Archive ×

Research Writing / 2025

The Dual Impact of Social Media

Research synthesis on connectivity, wellbeing and productivity.

This writing project examines how social media can support connection while raising questions about wellbeing, attention and productivity. The portfolio sample documents my research and revision process, rather than presenting a new empirical study.

FormatResearch proposal and argumentative essay
ProcessSource evaluation, synthesis and revision
Final EssayApril 25, 2025

Research Scope and Audience

The project asks how social media’s benefits and drawbacks can be considered together. Its final essay addresses a general audience, organizing the discussion around connection, productivity, different user experiences and proposed responses.

The writing task required a clear position while acknowledging competing perspectives.

Source Evaluation and Evidence Synthesis

The proposal establishes the initial question and scope. An eight source annotated bibliography evaluates each source’s argument, contribution, strengths, limitations and usefulness.

A literature review and source synthesis connect recurring ideas and opposing positions. The later addressing issues draft develops the structure that appears in the final essay.

Argument Structure and Editorial Decisions

The final essay moves from potential benefits to concerns about use, then considers differences between audiences and proposed responses. Plain language and descriptive headings help readers follow the argument.

The proposed responses span personal habits, digital literacy and platform responsibility. They are positions developed in an academic essay, not interventions evaluated in this project.

04 / Opening Excerpt
Social media is part of our everyday lives. Apps like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and LinkedIn help people stay in touch, share ideas, and discover new things. They let us connect with friends, family, classmates, coworkers, and even strangers from around the world.

Excerpt from the submitted final essay.

05 / Writing Samples

Read the proposal, annotated bibliography and final essay below.

Research Proposal

Research Proposal Draft

The Dual Impact of Social Media: Enhancing Connectivity or Deteriorating Mental Health and Productivity?

Section One: Research Question

How does social media simultaneously enhance global connectivity while negatively impacting mental health and productivity across different age groups?

In recent years, social media has emerged as a critical component of communication in the modern age, enabling connections across great distances, instant access to information, and interaction with diverse communities. While it has many benefits, including building relationships, creating educational materials, and aiding mental health organizations, it comes with serious downsides Many studies suggest that excessive social media use contributes to mental health issues, addiction-like behaviors, and decreased productivity in both academic and professional settings. The addictive design of social media platforms, driven by engagement-maximizing algorithms, encourages prolonged usage that may lead to negative cognitive and emotional effects. The purpose of this research is to investigate the dual role of social media: its advantages and disadvantages.

Section Two: Thesis Statement

While social media enhances communication and connectivity, its addictive design fosters anxiety, depression, and reduced productivity. A balanced approach—combining personal awareness, digital literacy, and policy regulation—is essential to mitigate its harms while maximizing its benefits.

Section Three: Context and Existing Research

Social Media’s Positive Impact

Social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok have transformed how people interact, offering spaces for self-expression, education, and professional networking. Research highlights that social media facilitates positive experiences, such as finding support groups, promoting mental health awareness, and fostering a sense of belonging among users (WJARR, 2024). Many businesses rely on social media for marketing, outreach, and customer engagement, demonstrating its significant economic impact. Additionally, sites like LinkedIn have promoted professional networking-allowing the job seekers to connect with prospective recruiters and major industry players globally. Moreover, social media is important in activism and political participation. Movements such as #MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, and climate change awareness went viral on social media. It was evident how, through social media, communities can be organized for social change. Studies have shown that this new generation, especially Generation Z and Millennials, are more into politics and social issues because of what they are exposed to online.

The Mental Health Risks of Social media

Social media also has several disadvantages, given that excessive use of it is associated with several negative psychological effects. In fact, research demonstrates a strong correlation between prolonged exposure to social media and increased levels of anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances, especially among young adults. The instant gratification model of likes, comments, and shares reinforces compulsive behaviors, leading to dependency and addiction-like symptoms. Continuous exposure to social media, which is edited, curated, and often unrealistic, breeds a toxic culture that hurts self-esteem in representations of success and beauty.

Of the many issues, one of the most disturbing is the impact of social media on adolescent mental health. According to studies, teenagers who spend over three hours daily on social media are more prone to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem (WJARR, 2024). Cyberbullying has also become rampant, with many young users experiencing online harassment, which can lead to emotional distress and, in severe cases, suicidal ideation.

Moreover, social media disrupts sleep patterns, which in turn exacerbates mental health issues. A study from the National Library of Medicine found that late-night social media usage is linked to poor sleep quality, daytime fatigue, and increased stress levels (Memon et al.). Sleep deprivation negatively impacts cognitive function, memory retention, and emotional regulation, further worsening users’ overall well-being.

The Effect of Social Media on Productivity

Social media has also raised concerns about decreased productivity in workplaces and educational institutions. The ease of accessing social media throughout the day leads to constant distractions, reduced focus, and procrastination. Studies from Harvard Business Review suggest that employees who frequently check social media during work hours have lower productivity levels and higher stress due to multitasking. Similarly, students who use social media excessively struggle with academic performance, lower grades, and decreased ability to retain information (VirtualMedHealth).

Furthermore, social media blurs the line between work and personal life, contributing to burnout. Many professionals feel pressure to remain constantly connected, checking work-related emails and messages outside of office hours, which diminishes work-life balance and leads to mental exhaustion.

Section Four: New Insight and Contribution

The purpose of this study is therefore to ascertain, through a qualitative approach, the dual impacts of social media on the age groups involved and at the same time develop strategic propositions for responsible use. While various studies have targeted either the benefits or drawbacks alone, the current study balances both sides to propose realistic strategies for responsible use of social media. This research will cover likely solutions that include: • Personal Awareness and Behavioral Changes: How people can be aware of their social media use, practice digital detox, and limit screen time. • Digital Literacy Programs: The role of education in driving healthier online behaviors, critical thinking to counter misinformation, and responsible engagement. • Regulatory and Ethical Considerations: Debate whether or not governments should implement strict regulations on social media platforms to prevent addictions due to algorithms and the theft of private user information. • Workplace and Educational Policies: Policies through which institutions can minimize productivity loss due to distractions caused by social media, such as limiting access during working hours or implementing focused work policy. This research will synthesize psychological, sociological, and technological findings to provide a comprehensive view of the effects of social media and make actionable recommendations for individuals, educators, policymakers, and businesses.

Conclusion

Social media has undoubtedly revolutionized communication, providing numerous benefits in terms of connectivity, information sharing, and professional growth. However, its overuse has raised serious concerns regarding mental health, addiction, and workplace/academic productivity. As digital platforms continue to evolve, it is crucial to find a balance that preserves their positive aspects while addressing their negative consequences. This research will provide insights into how social media affects different demographics and propose strategies to ensure that it remains a tool for enhancement rather than a source of harm.

Works Cited

Memon, Adeel M., et al. "The Impact of Social Media on Mental Health: A Narrative Review." National Library of Medicine, 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9915628/.

WJARR. "The Effects of Social Media on Mental Health and Productivity." World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, vol. 19, no. 2, 2024, pp. 45-60, https://wjarr.com/sites/default/files/WJARR-2024-3027.pdf.

VirtualMedHealth. "The Dual Impact of Social Media on Mental Health." VirtualMedHealth Blog, 2023, https://virtualmedhealth.com/blog/f/the-dual-impact-of-social-media-on-mental-health.

Annotated Bibliography and Literature Review

Annotated Bibliography

Abi-Jaoude, Elia, Karline Treurnicht Naylor, and Antonio Pignatiello. "Smartphones, Social Media Use and Youth Mental Health." CMAJ: Canadian Medical Association Journal, vol. 192, no. 6, 2020, pp. E136-E141, https://www.cmaj.ca/content/192/6/E136.

Main Argument: The authors discuss the association between increased smartphone and social media use among adolescents and the rise in mental distress, self-harming behaviors, and suicidality.

Contribution to Existing Research: This article synthesizes data from various studies to highlight the potential mental health risks associated with excessive social media use in teenagers.

Strengths and Limitations: The article provides a thorough review of existing literature but acknowledges the need for more longitudinal studies to establish causality.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is essential for understanding the potential negative impacts of social media on adolescent mental health, supporting discussions on the need for mindful usage.

Ajewumi, O. E., et al. "The Impact of Social Media on Mental Health and Well-being." World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, vol. 24, no. 1, 2024, pp. 107–121, https://wjarr.com/sites/default/files/WJARR-2024-3027.pdf.

Main Argument: The article explores both the positive and negative effects of social media on mental health, highlighting benefits like community building and self-expression, alongside drawbacks such as increased anxiety, depression, and loneliness due to social comparison and cyberbullying.

Contribution to Existing Research: This comprehensive review balances the dual impacts of social media, providing a nuanced perspective that encompasses both its advantages and disadvantages.

Strengths and Limitations: The article's balanced approach offers a holistic view; however, it relies heavily on existing literature without presenting new empirical data.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source supports the dual-impact framework of the research, offering insights into both the positive and negative consequences of social media usage.

Beyari, H. "The Relationship between Social Media and the Increase in Mental Health Problems." International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, vol. 20, no. 3, 2023, article 2383, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9915628/.

Main Argument: This study examines the correlation between social media usage and the rise in mental health issues among young adults, identifying specific features such as likes, comments, and followers as significant contributors to mental health deterioration.

Contribution to Existing Research: The research provides empirical evidence linking specific social media features to mental health problems, emphasizing the role of interactive elements in exacerbating anxiety and depression.

Strengths and Limitations: The study offers a detailed analysis using the Analytical Hierarchical Process (AHP) to assess the impact of various social media features. However, its focus on a specific demographic may limit the generalizability of the findings.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is valuable for discussing how particular social media features contribute to mental health issues, aligning with the negative aspects outlined in the research topic.

Keles, B., McCrae, N., and Grealish, A. "Social Media Use and Adolescent Mental Health: A Systematic Review." JMIR Mental Health, vol. 7, no. 6, 2020, article e17948, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7364393/.

Main Argument: The systematic review examines the association between social media use and mental health outcomes in adolescents, finding a significant correlation with increased depression and anxiety symptoms.

Contribution to Existing Research: This review consolidates findings from multiple studies, providing robust evidence of the negative mental health impacts of social media on adolescents.

Strengths and Limitations: The comprehensive nature of the review strengthens its conclusions, but the focus on adolescents may limit applicability to other age groups.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is essential for discussing age-specific vulnerabilities, particularly among adolescents, in the context of social media use.

Memon, Adeel M., et al. "The Impact of Social Media on Mental Health: A Narrative Review." Cureus, vol. 15, no. 1, 2023, article e34456, https://www.cureus.com/articles/176889-the-impact-of-social-media-on-the-mental-health-of-adolescents-and-young-adults-a-systematic-review.

Main Argument: This systematic review examines the relationship between social media usage and mental health among adolescents and young adults, identifying a significant association between increased social media use and mental distress, self-harming behaviors, and suicidality.

Contribution to Existing Research: The study consolidates findings from various research articles, providing a comprehensive overview of how excessive social media engagement correlates with adverse mental health outcomes in younger populations.

Strengths and Limitations: The review offers a thorough synthesis of existing literature, but its reliance on cross-sectional studies limits the ability to establish causality between social media use and mental health issues.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is valuable for understanding the potential negative impacts of social media on adolescent mental health, supporting discussions on the need for mindful usage.

"The Dual Impact of Social Media on Mental Health." Virtual Med Health, 2023, https://virtualmedhealth.com/blog/f/the-dual-impact-of-social-media-on-mental-health.

Main Argument: The article discusses how social media can serve as a platform for support and self-expression, while also posing risks such as fostering negative social comparisons and contributing to mental health issues.

Contribution to Existing Research: It offers insights into the dual nature of social media's impact, emphasizing the importance of mindful usage to harness benefits while mitigating risks.

Strengths and Limitations: The article provides practical recommendations but lacks empirical data to support its claims.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is useful for discussing practical strategies to balance the positive and negative effects of social media on mental health

"The Productivity Cost of Social Media at Work." Harvard Business Review, 2022, https://hbr.org/2022/03/the-productivity-cost-of-social-media-at-work.

Main Argument: The article examines how social media usage in the workplace can lead to decreased productivity due to distractions and multitasking.

Contribution to Existing Research: It provides an analysis of the economic implications of social media-induced productivity losses, offering data-driven insights into workplace behaviors.

Strengths and Limitations: The article presents real-world statistics and case studies but may not account for all variables influencing productivity, such as individual differences in self-control and job nature.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source is essential for discussing the impact of social media on workplace efficiency and productivity, providing a basis for recommendations on managing social media use in professional settings.

Twenge, Jean M., and W. Keith Campbell. "Associations Between Screen Time and Lower Psychological Well-Being Among Children and Adolescents: Evidence from a Population-Based Study." Preventive Medicine Reports, vol. 12, 2018, pp. 271-283.

Main Argument: The study examines the relationship between screen time, including social media use, and psychological well-being, finding that excessive screen time correlates with lower well-being in children and adolescents.

Contribution to Existing Research: It provides population-based evidence linking high screen time to adverse psychological outcomes in younger populations.

Strengths and Limitations: The large, representative sample strengthens the findings, but the study does not differentiate between types of screen time activities.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source supports arguments regarding the negative effects of excessive social media use on younger demographics.

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. "Social Media Use Can Be Positive for Mental Health and Well-Being." Harvard School of Public Health, 2023, https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/news/social-media-positive-mental-health/.

Main Argument: This article presents positive aspects of social media, arguing that it can help individuals feel connected, provide emotional support, and improve mental well-being.

Contribution to Existing Research: The article highlights how social media can serve as a tool for mental health support, rather than just a risk factor.

Strengths and Limitations: It presents real-world benefits but does not include experimental studies to support its claims.

Usefulness for Research Paper: This source helps balance the argument by showing how social media can be used in a beneficial way.

Literature Review

The Impact of Social Media on Mental Health

Introduction

Social media has become a major part of daily life, especially for young people. While it helps people stay connected, research shows that excessive use can harm mental health. This literature review explores how social media affects mental well-being, highlighting what researchers agree on, where they differ, and what gaps still exist in current studies.

What Researchers Have Found

Many studies agree that spending too much time on social media can lead to mental health issues. Abi-Jaoude et al. (2020) state, “There is a strong link between increased social media use and rising levels of mental distress, self-harm, and suicidality among adolescents.” Twenge and Campbell (2018) add that excessive screen time "reduces real-life interactions, which are essential for mental well-being.”

However, some research suggests that social media can improve mental health. Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2023) argues, “For many, social media is a space where they can express themselves, find support groups, and stay socially connected." This suggests that how social media is used—rather than just time spent—determines its impact.

Beyari (2023) expands on these ideas by discussing the impact of negative content and cyberbullying on mental health. The study explains that "social media algorithms are designed to reinforce user engagement by continuously showing content similar to what individuals interact with", which means that users who engage with harmful or distressing content are likely to see more of it, potentially worsening their mental state. Similarly, Keles et al. (2020) reviewed multiple studies and found that social media does not affect everyone in the same way, stating that "while some individuals experience heightened levels of anxiety and depression, others find emotional support and a sense of belonging through online communities." This suggests that the way people engage with social media—rather than just the amount of time spent—plays a critical role in determining its mental health effects.

Differences and Contradictions in Research

Researchers disagree on the primary cause of social media’s impact on mental health. Some, like Twenge & Campbell (2018), argue that "higher screen time is directly linked to lower psychological well-being in children and adolescents," suggesting that time spent on social media itself is harmful. Others, such as Keles et al. (2020), counter that "the type of content consumed, rather than the total time spent, plays a more significant role in determining mental health outcomes." Additionally, while some studies claim that social media always negatively affects mental health, others highlight its positive aspects. For example, Ajewumi et al. (2024) state, "Social media platforms provide opportunities for community-building, self-expression, and emotional support, which can reduce feelings of loneliness and social isolation." These conflicting perspectives suggest that the effects of social media vary depending on how individuals engage with it.

Gaps in Existing Research

Although extensive research explores the negative impact of social media, there are still critical gaps. First, most studies focus on adolescents, leaving a gap in understanding how social media affects older populations. Keles et al. (2020) acknowledge that "while adolescent mental health has been extensively studied in relation to social media, there is limited data on its impact on adults and elderly users." Second, there is not enough focus on how different types of content (positive vs. negative) affect mental health. As Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2023) states, "Social media can promote positive mental well-being when used for connection and self-expression, but harmful when it fosters unrealistic social comparisons." Finally, many studies rely on self-reported data, which may not always be reliable. As Beyari (2023) warns, "Self-reported measures of social media use are often inconsistent and may not accurately reflect actual engagement patterns." Future research should focus on studying various age groups, analyzing content differences, and using experimental studies to understand the true impact of social media on mental health.

Conclusion

The research clearly shows that social media can impact mental health, but its effects depend on how individuals use it. While some studies emphasize its risks, others highlight its potential benefits. Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2023) explains, "Social media, when used mindfully, can enhance well-being by fostering connections and reducing social isolation." Future research should explore how different individuals experience social media differently, focusing on healthy engagement strategies to maximize benefits while minimizing harm.

Final Essay

This is a big issue for many different people. Teenagers, adults, older adults, all use social media, but not everyone understands how it affects them. Some feel connected and supported. Others feel lonely, anxious, or distracted. In this essay, I will explain both the good and bad sides of social media. I will also offer ideas on how we can use social media in a healthier way. By sharing new ways to solve the problems, we can help make social media a better place for everyone.

The Good Side of Social Media

Social media can be very helpful. First, it helps us stay connected with people. If your family or friends live far away, social media can make it easy to talk to them. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when people couldn’t meet in person, social media helped people stay in touch and not feel alone. According to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, social media can help people feel more supported and less lonely. It can also improve mental health when used the right way. Second, social media is a great place to find support groups. People dealing with similar problems can talk to each other, share advice, and feel less alone. According to Ajewumi et al., social media helps with building communities, sharing emotions, and self-expression. It gives people a place where they can be themselves. Third, social media helps raise awareness about important topics. Movements like #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter became stronger because people could share stories and information on social media. These platforms let people speak up every day and create real change in society.

Finally, social media helps people find jobs and grow businesses. LinkedIn helps professionals connect with employers. Small businesses use Instagram or Facebook to advertise and sell products. People also learn new skills through short videos or online classes shared on social media.

The Harmful Side of Social Media

Even though social media has good parts, it also has a dark side. Spending too much time online can hurt our minds. Many studies show that too much time on social media can make people feel more anxious, sad, or lonely. For example, Abi-Jaoude et al. found that teenagers who use social media a lot have more mental health problems. They may feel depressed or even hurt themselves. Social media platforms are made to keep us online. Every time we get a like or comment, our brain feels good. That makes us want to keep checking the app. Beyari explains that social media shows us more of what we already look at. This means people might keep seeing sad or harmful content again and again, without even realizing it.

Another problem is cyberbullying. Many people, especially teens, get bullied online. Negative comments or mean messages can make people feel terrible. VirtualMedHealth says that online bullying can cause serious mental health problems. Also, when people use social media late at night, they sleep less. Without enough sleep, people feel tired, stressed, and moody the next day. Social media also spreads false information very fast. This can be especially confusing for older adults, who might believe something that’s not true. Misinformation can cause stress, fear, or even harm to people’s health or relationships.

How Social Media Hurts Productivity

Social media doesn’t just hurt mental health, it can also hurt focus. Students who use social media a lot during school have a hard time paying attention. They may get lower grades or take longer to finish their work. VirtualMedHealth found that these students often struggle with schoolwork. At work, people also get distracted. The Harvard Business Review says that social media makes people multitask more. This means they switch between tasks too often, which lowers the quality of their work. Some workers also keep checking social media after work, which can lead to stress and burnout. Also, when people try to work or study and check their phones at the same time, their brain works harder. They become more tired and less productive. Many people don’t realize how much time they waste on social media, and it takes away from their focus and creativity.

Different Effects for Different People

Not everyone uses social media the same way, and not everyone is affected the same way. Teenagers often face peer pressure and are more likely to be bullied online. Young adults might compare their lives to what they see online and feel bad about themselves. Older adults may feel lonely, but they use social media to stay in touch with family. However, they are also more likely to believe fake news. Keles et al. explain that some people feel worse when they use social media, but others feel better. For example, someone might find comfort in talking to friends online. Someone else might feel sad when they see pictures of other people’s perfect lives. Knowing these differences is important. We can use this information to create better solutions that help everyone.

New Solutions: How We Can Use Social Media Better

We can enjoy the benefits of social media without letting it hurt us. Here are some ideas:

1. Watch your habits: People can track how much time they spend online. Many phones have settings that let you set limits. Taking breaks, especially before bed, can protect your mental health and improve sleep.

2. Teach smart usage: Schools and jobs should teach people how to use social media in a safe and smart way. People should learn how to tell if something is false. They should also learn how social media apps are designed and how they can affect emotions.

3. Stronger rules: Governments and tech companies should make better rules. For example, they can remove endless scrolling or add warnings for harmful content. They should also protect people’s private information.

4. Focus zones: Schools and workplaces can set up phone-free zones or “digital detox” days. This helps people stay focused and reduces stress.

5. Online mental health support: Social media apps can offer links to mental health resources. If someone is feeling upset or in danger, they should be able to get help quickly through the app. These simple steps can help people use social media in a healthier way. We do not need to stop using social media completely, we just need to use it more wisely.

Bringing New Ideas to the Conversation

A lot of people have talked about the good and bad sides of social media. But what we need now is action. We need to focus on creating tools and lessons that help different people based on their needs. For example, teenagers need protection from bullying. Adults need help with work-life balance. Older adults need help spotting false information. Each group needs a different strategy. We can also build better apps. App designers should stop trying to make people stay online forever. Instead, they can create apps that encourage people to take breaks, learn something new, or connect in positive ways. If people start asking for healthier social media tools, companies will listen. The government can also make a difference. It can pass laws that protect users. For example, it can make sure social media companies report how their apps affect mental health. If people know what’s really going on behind the screen, they can make better choices. Most importantly, we need to talk more about these problems. Many people don’t even realize how social media is affecting their lives. If we share stories, research, and ideas, we can help others become more aware. Talking is the first step to change.

Conclusion

Social media is a powerful tool. It helps us connect, share ideas, and learn new things. But it also comes with risks. It can hurt our minds, distract us from school or work, and make us feel worse about ourselves. Different people are affected in different ways, and we need to create smart solutions that help everyone. By watching our habits, learning how to use social media wisely, and building better rules and tools, we can enjoy the good parts of social media while avoiding the bad ones. This is something we all need to work on: students, teachers, parents, tech companies, and leaders. If we all work together, we can make social media a safer, smarter, and healthier part of our lives.

Argument / 2024

Free College Education in the United States

Policy argument on education access and funding allocation.

An argumentative essay proposing that public tuition support should follow students to their chosen college. The companion bibliography documents the sources used to develop the position.

AuthorGazala Shaikh
DeliverablePolicy analysis and source evaluation
ContextWriting portfolio

Composition and Editorial Approach

A position supported through examples and source discussion.

Original compositions and supporting research are available below.

Read the Essay

Imagine a country where every student has the freedom to pursue higher education without the crushing burden of tuition fees. Picture a system where students choose the college that best fits their dreams, whether it is public or private, without worrying about cost or admission caps. It is not just about reducing student debt or creating a stronger workforce; it is about fairness, opportunity, and the belief that education should be a right, not a privilege. The United States has long valued the idea of equal opportunity, but the high cost of college has created a barrier for many. Government funding should follow students directly to their chosen college, giving them the opportunity to learn and grow without financial roadblocks. If the government can spend billions or even trillions of dollars on wars abroad, it can and should invest in its people by funding free college and improving the lives of millions of Americans.

Imagine a student who dreams of attending a specialized art program at a private college but cannot afford the tuition. Under this model, the government would pay the tuition directly to that college. Scott Blankenbiller, in Free College Tuition is Good for America, explains how free education would reduce student debt and allow young people to focus on building their futures. Instead of limiting choices to public colleges with overcrowded classrooms, students could pick the program that truly matches their goals. Allowing funding to follow students would also take the pressure off public colleges, which are often overwhelmed with applications. Laura W. Perna and Edward J. Smith, in The Path to Free College: In Pursuit of Access, Equity, and Prosperity, show how programs like the “Promise Programs” have increased enrollment and provided better outcomes for students. Expanding this model to include private colleges would open even more doors. With more options available, students could find schools that align with their unique career paths, whether that is engineering, nursing, or fine arts.

One question people often ask is, “How will we pay for this?” But the better question is, “Why are we spending trillions on wars and defense while ignoring education?” Research from Free College Now highlights how educated citizens contribute to the economy through higher earnings, increased tax revenue, and reduced reliance on government assistance. Investing in free college is not a handout; it is a smart financial decision. Redirecting even a small portion of defense spending toward education could change millions of lives and strengthen the country. Tressie McMillan Cottom, in her article "Why Free College Is Necessary," emphasizes the broader societal benefits of free college. Cottom argues that free tuition represents a public investment in human potential and ensures education is accessible to everyone. By tying government funding to students rather than institutions, we can create a system where individual ambitions are supported, and no one is forced to forgo their dreams because of financial limitations.

Another benefit of trying to fund students is that it would push colleges to improve. Schools would need to attract students by offering better programs, facilities, and faculty. This competition would create a system where every institution works harder to provide a quality education. To ensure accountability, the government could require schools to maintain reasonable tuition rates and high academic standards. This way, the funds would be used to directly benefit students, not pay college budgets. Free college education would also address workforce shortages in key industries. Careers in healthcare, education, and technology need skilled professionals, but many students are scared away by the cost of degrees. Imagine how many nurses we could train if tuition was not a barrier. Teaching programs could attract more students, helping solve the teacher shortage across the country. By covering tuition costs, we could encourage more young people to pursue degrees in these essential fields, filling gaps that hurt communities today.

This model would also give students access to specialized programs at private institutions. Not all colleges are created equal; some offer unique courses that cannot be found elsewhere. A student passionate about marine biology might want to attend a college with cutting-edge facilities for ocean research, while another might prefer a film school known for its connections to the entertainment industry. By allowing funding to follow the student, we empower individuals to choose the path that excites and motivates them most. However, free college is not just about covering tuition. Students need support to succeed. Academic advisors, mental health counselors, and career coaches are essential for helping students navigate the challenges of higher education. Perna and Smith emphasize that these resources make a huge difference in student success. When combined with financial aid, they ensure students not only enroll in college but also thrive and graduate. The benefits of free college education extend far beyond the classroom. An educated population is more likely to vote, volunteer, and contribute to their communities. Colleges would become centers of innovation, where students could freely explore ideas, start businesses, and develop solutions to global challenges like climate change or economic inequality. Without the constant stress of debt, students could focus on what matters most, which is learning and creating.

This system would also uplift underserved areas. Many students in rural or low-income communities struggle to access higher education due to financial constraints or limited options nearby. Free college would give them the freedom to attend schools that meet their needs, bringing new opportunities to communities that have been overlooked for far too long. Imagine the impact if more students from these regions became teachers, doctors, or entrepreneurs, bringing change back to their hometowns. Some worry that free colleges might lower the value of degrees or encourage colleges to cut corners. These concerns are valid, but they can be addressed with proper planning. Colleges could be required to meet quality standards, and government audits could ensure funds are being used effectively. Additionally, tying funding to graduation rates or job placements would keep institutions focused on delivering real results for students.

The vision of free college education is both achievable and essential. It is a solution that addresses workforce shortages, strengthens the economy, and opens doors for millions of students to achieve their dreams. By redirecting resources from unnecessary expenditures, like wars, to meaningful investments in education, the government can build a future that benefits everyone. Free college is not just about removing debt; it is about creating a fair system that values learning and opportunity for all. The time has come for the United States to embrace this change and make education accessible to every student, regardless of their financial situation.

A Serene Retreat: Observing the Heart of My Home:

The living room is the heart of any home, and mine is no different. Sunlight gently filters through the wide windows, casting a soft, warm glow across my living room. The beige couches, arranged thoughtfully around a sleek fireplace, invite a sense of solace and tranquility. A large wooden world map decorates the wall, adding a sense of adventure and peculiarity to the room. The coffee table and stools sit neatly in the center, offering a simple yet functional gathering spot. Nearby, the dining table stands ready for family meals, making the living room feel complete. Thanks to the open-concept design, the living room flows smooth into the kitchen, allowing the two areas to connect in a natural, uninterrupted way. This layout makes it ideal for hosting gatherings or simply enjoying family time without feeling divided by walls. The soft colors and clean lines give the room a peaceful, airy feel. Every detail, from the choice of decor to the arrangement of furniture, speaks to a thoughtful design. The living room is more than a place to sit; it is a retreat where comfort and style come together.

In the living room, comfort and style go hand in hand. The beige couches are like soft clouds, inviting anyone to sink in and relax. They are thoughtfully arranged around the room's focal point, with a large wooden world map hanging above the main sofa, adding a touch of adventure, even if the farthest journey taken lately is just to the grocery store. A TV sits prominently on the wall, with a stylish table below it that serves as both a soundbar stand and a storage spot, filled with toys belonging to my two boys. In the center, a coffee table and stools are ready for snacks, games, or a pile of books waiting to be explored. The space feels calm and welcoming, with every piece of furniture in its perfect spot. Nearby, the dining table is set for family dinners or casual conversations. The room manages to feel simple yet exciting, resembling a laid-back hangout that doesn’t have to try too hard. Wide windows let sunlight pour in, casting a warm glow that transforms the space into a cozy oasis. Each item serves a purpose, and together, they create a sense of completeness.

Altogether, the living room serves as more than just a functional space; it is a true retreat where every detail contributes to an atmosphere of peace, comfort, and warmth. The fireplace, with its carefully selected mantel decor, stands as the perfect finishing touch, adding a sense of intimacy and style to the room. The smooth marble finish of the fireplace complements the room’s overall minimalist design, while the delicate items atop the mantel such as a small bicycle figurine, potted plants, and other personal touches—offer subtle yet thoughtful decoration. These items add a sense of charm without detracting from the room's sleek, modern aesthetic. They provide just the right balance of simplicity and personality, making the room feel both lived-in and elegant. The fireplace itself is not only functional, offering warmth during colder months, but it also serves as a gathering point, drawing people toward its inviting glow. On chilly evenings, the warmth of the fire becomes the heart of the room, encouraging family members to come together and share cozy moments.

One of the standout features of the home is the effortless connection between the living room and kitchen. Without walls to divide them, laughter and chatter flow freely, fostering an inviting atmosphere. It appears the walls of the house encourage everyone to come together and share their experiences. Whether someone is chopping vegetables at the kitchen counter or lounging comfortably on the couch, the energy in the room remains lively and friendly. This open layout promotes inclusivity, allowing everyone to engage in conversations, regardless of their location in the room. The space is alive with warmth, making it an ideal backdrop for family gatherings and casual evenings with friends. Here, cherished memories are created over shared meals and stories. The design masterfully combines practicality with comfort, ensuring the area is suitable for any occasion. In this special room, the simple act of being together elevates everyday moments into treasured experiences.

The living room’s color palette, featuring beige, white, and warm brown creates a calming vibe that instantly puts you at ease. It is bright, open, and feels like the kind of place where you can breathe easily. It is designed to make you feel comfortable. But here is the magic: this room is not just a pretty space; it makes everyday moments feel a bit more special. Imagine a bright morning with sunlight streaming through the windows, it is like the whole room is waking up with you. And on chilly evenings, the fireplace casts a soft, warm glow, turning the room into the coziest spot in the house. Whether you are having a family movie night, sharing stories with friends, or just kicking back with a book, the room adapts to the moment. It feels alive with energy, but also like a place where you can simply relax and be yourself. What really makes this space stand out are the little personal touches, like the world map hanging on the wall and the quirky decor on the mantel. They are not just random decor pieces; they represent memories and experiences, making the space feel like it holds a piece of everyone who spends time there.

This living room is more than just a room, it is the heart and soul of the home. It is where life unfolds, where laughter echoes, where quiet moments feel peaceful, and where memories are made. Whether it is filled with people or just a quiet evening alone, the room always feels inviting, wrapping you in a sense of coziness and comfort. Every detail, from the furniture to the decor, is there for a reason, creating a space that is functional yet full of life. It is the kind of place that makes even the simplest moments feel special, where everything comes together, and home truly feels like home.

My First Pregnancy Experience

A learning narrative organized around uncertainty, support and a major personal transition. The finished essay builds on earlier topic exploration, an opening draft and supporting paragraphs.

AuthorGazala Shaikh
DeliverableNarrative composition and editorial development
ContextWriting portfolio

Composition and Editorial Approach

Chronology, dialogue and reflection connect the experience to what the writer learned.

Original compositions and supporting research are available below.

Read the Learning Narrative

I thought a regular doctor’s visit could not get more dramatic, but November 21, 2017, proved me wrong. My usual doctor was on vacation, and a nurse practitioner stepped in to shake things up. “Your baby’s heartbeat is not quite right. We might need to admit you.” After an hour of tense monitoring and feeling like a ticking time bomb, they sent me home—turns out, that was just a drill. On November 25, the day the real contractions began, and by night, I ended up screaming in the car like I was in a dramatic movie. The real challenge of childbirth had begun. This crazy day showed me childbirth is full of surprises, but the kindness around you makes every moment priceless.

By the morning of November 25th, I could tell something was different. The contractions started early and kept coming all day, but they never seemed close enough to rush to the hospital. I had already gone to the hospital on the evening of November 24th, but it turned out to be a false alarm. I tried everything I could think of to help with the pain; walking around the house, pacing back and forth, and taking warm baths—but nothing worked. Every minute felt like an hour, and I was stuck waiting, knowing my baby was coming but not knowing when things would really begin. The waiting felt endless, and I kept looking at the clock, hoping time would go faster. By 11 PM, the pain became so strong that I could no longer handle it. My husband quickly helped me into the car, and each bump in the road made me scream. He drove as fast as he could, and I held on, trying to breathe and scream through the pain. Throughout this ordeal, my mother and grandmother kept calling me from India, offering their unwavering support and encouragement. Their voices, despite the distance, provided me with a sense of strength and comfort.

As soon as we stepped out of the elevator, all the nurses’ attention turned to me. The same nurse from the previous night rushed over with a wheelchair and said, “Now you are ready!” She moved quickly to get me to the labor room. Everything felt fast-paced and urgent, and I was feeling more and more overwhelmed. The other nurse asked me, “On a scale of 1 to 10, how much pain are you in for the epidural?” I was lost, this was my first pregnancy! I had no idea what a six or a ten felt like, and I did not even really understand what an epidural was supposed to do. All I knew was that I was in a lot of pain and needed relief. I said, “I do not know, just give me something to help!” The nurse gently guided me, holding me steady and wrapping her arms around me. I was shaking from the pain and fear, but her presence made me feel a bit more secure.

After the epidural started to take effect, I felt an incredible wave of relaxation wash over me. Even though I was still connected to various wires and machines, and the contractions were still happening, the intense pain had finally eased. My lower half was numb, and it felt like a warm, comforting blanket had been draped over me. The world around me seemed to slow down, and I could finally think clearly. The relief was so profound that I could almost forget about the contractions, even though they were still there, now more like distant waves rather than crashing storms. I watched as the nurses and doctors moved around, their faces focused and calm, and I felt a sense of peace despite the busy atmosphere. It was a strange but welcome sensation; pain had transformed into a dull ache, and I felt much more in control, ready to face whatever came next in this childbirth adventure.

Then, as if sensing my thoughts, my husband came over and held my hand. His presence was calming, and seeing the worry in his eyes somehow reassured me. I was not alone. He had been there for me through every moment, from the late-night hospital visits to this final, intense moment. His quiet strength gave me the boost I needed to keep going. And his own “booster”? It was the double espresso shot he had, something he had only ever taken twice in his life; once during the birth of our first son, which is now, and, for our second.

As the hours passed, the atmosphere became more intense. The doctors told me I was fully dilated, and it was time to push. A surge of fear hit me. Despite the epidural, I could still feel the immense pressure, and the task ahead seemed overwhelming. The room was filled with seven or eight nurses, all working together to manage the delivery. Their voices blended as they encouraged me to push, guiding me through each moment. The energy in the room was intense, yet focused, and their support was constant as they handled every detail of the process, helping me bring my baby into the world. After what felt like forever, I finally heard the most beautiful sound: my baby’s first cry.

That tiny, strong cry broke through the exhaustion and pain, filling me with joy and relief. My husband, smiling with pride, cut the umbilical cord; a moment that felt like he was the one welcoming our baby into the world. Right after that, they placed my baby on my chest. His eyes were tightly closed, so I could not see them right away. In fact, I did not get a good look at his eyes until a few hours later. But even then, I already knew he was a little version of me; my mini-me. The medical staff kept watching over us, making sure both the baby and I were okay. My body was completely tired, like I had just run a marathon, but at the same time, I had this strange energy. The adrenaline kept me wide awake, and even though I had been through the hardest physical experience of my life, I could not stop looking at my baby.

My grandmother, my father, my mother, and the rest of my family were overjoyed as they met this tiny version of me through video call, their happiness radiating through every call and message. Seeing how much love and excitement he brought to my family made everything feel even more special. He was not just a new baby; he was the continuation of a legacy, a new chapter in our family’s story. The moment carried even more significance because I had been the first child in the new generation of my family, and now he was the beginning of the next.

When the nurses took him for his first checks and measurements, I felt a small pang of separation. This tiny little one was more than just my child; he was a part of me, reminding me of my journey and dreams. The chaos of labor faded away, replaced by the warmth of my family’s love and the excitement of new beginnings. Each call and message from my loved ones made me feel so connected, bridging the miles between us with joy. My baby marked the start of a new chapter in our family story, continuing the legacy of those who came before us. I could already imagine the stories he would hear, the laughter we would share, and the special moments we would create together. As I looked down at my sleeping bundle of joy after the nurses laid him in the crib, I knew our adventure was just beginning, filled with love and endless possibilities. This moment was not just about his birth; it was the start of a beautiful future for our family.

My First Pregnancy Experience:

I thought a regular doctor’s visit couldn’t get more dramatic, but November 21, 2017, proved me wrong. My usual doctor was on vacation, and a nurse practitioner stepped in to shake things up: “Your baby’s heartbeat isn’t quite right. We might need to admit you.” After an hour of tense monitoring and feeling like a ticking time bomb, they sent me home—turns out, that was just a drill. On November 25, the day of real contractions began, and by night, I ended up screaming in the car like I was in a dramatic movie. The real challenge of childbirth had begun. This crazy day showed me how unpredictable childbirth can be, how amazing the people in the delivery room can be and no matter how wild the journey, it’s worth every moment for the result.
